presentingComplaint: Progressive generalised swelling and frothy urine on the 6th day after elective total knee replacement.
history: A 73-year-old man is reviewed on the orthopaedic ward on post-operative day 6 following an uncomplicated elective right total knee replacement. Over the preceding 3-4 days he has developed progressively worsening bilateral leg and periorbital swelling, tight-fitting shoes, an 4 kg weight gain, and notably frothy, foaming urine. He denies chest pain, orthopnoea that predates admission, or reduced urine output, though he feels increasingly breathless on minimal exertion. Background: type 2 diabetes mellitus (12 years, on metformin), hypertension, osteoarthritis and mild diverticular disease. His inpatient drug chart shows polypharmacy - regular diclofenac and additional PRN ibuprofen for post-operative analgesia (started at surgery), enoxaparin prophylaxis, omeprazole, amlodipine, ramipril and atorvastatin. He has no prior renal disease documented and a normal pre-operative creatinine and urinalysis. No fever, rash, joint pains, haematuria or recent sore throat. Non-smoker; no history of hepatitis or heavy alcohol use.
examination: Comfortable at rest but mildly breathless on lying flat. Marked pitting oedema to the thighs bilaterally with periorbital puffiness and mild scrotal oedema. Abdomen soft, non-tender, with shifting dullness suggesting modest ascites. Chest: reduced air entry and stony dullness at both bases consistent with small pleural effusions; no crepitations of pulmonary oedema. JVP not elevated. Heart sounds normal, no added sounds or murmur. Surgical wound clean and dry with no surrounding erythema. No focal neurology, no calf tenderness or asymmetric limb swelling.

labs.urinalysis: 3+ protein, no blood, no cells, bland sediment with occasional oval fat bodies / fatty casts

imaging: Chest radiograph: small bilateral pleural effusions with clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys (10.9 and 11.2 cm) with preserved cortical thickness and no obstruction, supporting a medical rather than obstructive cause.
microbiology: Not indicated - no clinical features of infection; wound swab and blood cultures not required. Urine culture negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia) - likely NSAID-associated (minimal change / membranous) versus underlying diabetic nephropathy
Decompensated congestive cardiac failure with anasarca
Hepatic cirrhosis with hypoalbuminaemia and ascites
Acute kidney injury from peri-operative NSAID/ACE-inhibitor exposure
Deep vein thrombosis (unilateral limb swelling) - excluded by bilateral symmetric oedema
finalDiagnosis: Nephrotic syndrome (nephrotic-range proteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia <3.0 g/dL, oedema and hyperlipidaemia), precipitated in an elderly polypharmacy patient by peri-operative NSAID exposure on a background of diabetes; requires drug withdrawal and nephrology work-up including consideration of renal biopsy.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Glomerular Diseases / Nephrotic Syndrome
stewardship: Non-infective presentation - no antimicrobial therapy indicated. Antimicrobial stewardship point: resist the reflex to start empiric antibiotics for 'post-operative swelling and breathlessness' when there is no fever, leucocytosis, wound or urinary source; the frothy urine, hypoalbuminaemia and nephrotic-range proteinuria point to a renal, non-infective diagnosis. Note that nephrotic patients are functionally immunocompromised (urinary immunoglobulin/complement loss) and at risk of pneumococcal peritonitis/sepsis, so pneumococcal vaccination and vigilance for genuine infection are appropriate, but no empiric antibiotic is warranted here.
contraindications: Continued NSAIDs (diclofenac/ibuprofen) - stop immediately as the likely precipitant and nephrotoxin
ACE inhibitor (ramipril) should be reviewed/held during acute kidney injury and volume shifts, then reintroduced for anti-proteinuric benefit once stable
Nephrotoxic contrast and aminoglycosides given reduced eGFR
Aggressive diuresis risking intravascular depletion and worsening AKI/thrombosis
edgeCases: Nephrotic syndrome markedly increases venous thromboembolism risk (urinary antithrombin loss) - a superimposed DVT/PE or renal vein thrombosis can confound the peri-operative picture
In the elderly, membranous nephropathy may be paraneoplastic - a malignancy screen is warranted
Diabetic nephropathy can coexist; absence of retinopathy and the abrupt onset with NSAID use favour a superimposed drug-induced lesion, which may need biopsy to distinguish
Serum albumin and total protein can be spuriously interpreted; hypoalbuminaemia here is renal loss, not hepatic synthetic failure or malnutrition
expectedMaiK: Recognise nephrotic syndrome from the triad of nephrotic-range proteinuria (frothy urine, UPCR 7.8, 24h protein 6.4 g), hypoalbuminaemia (1.9 g/dL) and generalised oedema with hyperlipidaemia; stop the offending NSAIDs, review the ACE inhibitor, and arrange nephrology assessment with a secondary-cause work-up and consideration of renal biopsy - not antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the exact timing and dose of NSAID exposure relative to symptom onset?
Is there any preceding proteinuria, foamy urine, or oedema before this admission?
Any features of malignancy (weight loss, lymphadenopathy) or systemic disease (rash, arthralgia) suggesting a secondary cause?
Any unilateral limb swelling, pleuritic pain or breathlessness suggesting VTE, given the prothrombotic nephrotic state?
expectedInvestigations: Quantify proteinuria: urine protein:creatinine ratio and/or 24-hour urine protein
Serum albumin, renal function/eGFR and fasting lipid profile
Urinalysis with microscopy for oval fat bodies and to exclude an active (nephritic) sediment
Secondary-cause serology: HbA1c, ANA/complement, hepatitis B/C, serum/urine electrophoresis and anti-PLA2R antibody
Renal ultrasound to confirm size and exclude obstruction; renal biopsy for definitive histological diagnosis
Doppler/VTE assessment given the prothrombotic nephrotic state
regressionAssertions: Engine should return nephrotic as the top diagnosis given nephrotic-range proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema + hyperlipidaemia.
No antibiotics should be recommended (infective:false; tier null).
Discontinuation of NSAIDs and review of ACE inhibitor must appear in management.
Differential should include heart_failure, decomp_cirrhosis, ckd and aki but not rank them above nephrotic.
Renal biopsy and secondary-cause work-up should be proposed among investigations.
